messages.content: My cousins are coming for Diwali and I have to plan one evening for everyone. Any ideas?

A simple plan works best with a mixed group. You could start by lighting diyas together, then hold a rangoli contest in teams, and finish with dinner and sweets. How many people are coming, and what ages are they?
About twelve people. The youngest is five and my grandmother is eighty.

Then make the rangoli teams mixed, so each child works with an adult. Your grandmother could be the judge, which keeps her at the centre without tiring her out. Save the crackers for the end, and keep the five-year-old at a safe distance with an adult beside him.
I have a maths test on Friday and I keep putting off studying.
That happens to a lot of people, especially when a subject feels heavy. Which part of the test worries you most?
Fractions. I understand them in class but forget everything at home.

That usually means you need practice, not more reading. Try five fraction problems each evening until Friday, and check your answers straight away. Small daily practice sticks better than one long session.
Five a day sounds doable. What if I get them wrong?

Getting them wrong is part of the practice. Look at where the mistake happened, fix it, and try one more of the same kind. If a problem still confuses you by Wednesday, take it to your teacher on Thursday. That still leaves time before the test.
My best friend didn't talk to me all day at school. I don't know what I did.
That feels confusing and a little lonely. It might not be about you at all. She could be worried about something at home, or just tired. Did anything happen between you two recently?
Not that I remember. Should I just ask her?

Yes, a gentle question is often the kindest way. You could say, "You seemed quiet today. Is everything okay?" Ask when you two are alone, and give her time to answer. If she is not ready to talk, let her know you are around when she is.
I want to cook dinner for my parents tonight. I can only make dal and rice.
Dal and rice is a comforting meal, and parents usually love being cooked for. You could add one simple side to make it feel special.
Like what? I don't want anything difficult.
A cucumber and onion salad with lemon and salt takes ten minutes and needs no stove. Or you could serve plain curd with a pinch of roasted cumin.
I'll do the salad. Should I make it before or after the dal?
Make it last, just before serving. Cut cucumber goes watery if it sits too long. Put the dal on first, then the rice, and make the salad while they cook.
Okay. My mother likes her dal less salty, by the way.

Then add less salt than you normally would and taste it near the end. Put a little salt on the table so others can add more. That way your mother's plate is just right, and nobody else has to eat it bland.
I start my first job on Monday. I'm nervous about not knowing anyone.
Most people feel that way on day one, even if they hide it. Remember that your new team expects you to be new. Nobody thinks you should know everything yet.
How do I start talking to people without it being awkward?

Start small. Learn two or three names in the morning and use them later. Asking someone, "How long have you worked here?" or "Where do people usually have lunch?" opens an easy conversation. Joining others for lunch in the first week helps a lot.
We're going to Shimla next month. It's my first time in the mountains.
How exciting. Mountain towns are lovely, and the cool air feels very different from the plains. Do you know what the weather will be like then?
It'll be December, so cold I think.

Yes, December is cold there, and it may even snow. Pack layers: a warm jacket, a sweater, thermal wear, woollen socks and a cap. Layers are better than one heavy coat because you can take some off indoors.
Do I need special shoes?
Shoes with a good grip are a smart choice, because roads and steps can be slippery with frost. Avoid smooth soles. Waterproof shoes are even better if you can borrow a pair.
My little brother is coming too. He's seven.

Then pack extra socks and gloves for him, since children often get their hands and feet wet while playing. Keep a small bag with snacks and a water bottle, because walks between places take longer on hills.
Any idea what we could do there with him?

An easy walk with views of the valley suits a seven-year-old well. If there is snow, building a small snowman will probably be his favourite part. Keep the plans light, with rest breaks, so nobody gets too tired.
Everyone in my class went to a birthday party on Sunday and I wasn't invited.
I'm sorry. Finding out you were left out hurts, especially when everyone else seems to be talking about it.
Now they keep showing photos at lunch and I feel stupid.
You are not stupid for feeling hurt. It's a normal reaction. Sometimes parties are kept small because of space or cost, and the host may not have meant it as a message about you.
Maybe. What should I do at lunch tomorrow?

You could sit with one or two people you get along with and bring up a different topic, like a show or the homework. If the photos come out again, it's fine to say, "Looks fun," and move on. If the sadness stays with you, talking to a parent or a teacher you trust can really help.
We just got a puppy and he cries every night.
That's very common in the first weeks. He has just left his mother and siblings, so the nights feel strange and lonely to him.
Is there something we can do so he settles down?

Put his bed in a quiet corner near where someone sleeps, so he can hear you. A soft blanket or an old T-shirt that smells of your family can comfort him. Take him out just before bedtime too. Most puppies settle within a few weeks.
I didn't get selected for the school cricket team.
That's disappointing, especially if you practised hard for it. How are you feeling about it?
Bad. My friend got in and I didn't.
It can sting more when a friend makes it and you don't. You can be happy for him and still feel sad for yourself. Both feelings are allowed.
The coach said my fielding needs work.
That's useful, even if it hurts to hear. Fielding improves a lot with regular practice. Catching a tennis ball off a wall for ten minutes a day can make a real difference.
Trials are again in six months.

Six months is plenty of time to improve your fielding. You could ask the coach for one or two drills he likes, and maybe practise with your friend now that he's in the team. Then go back to trials with something new to show.
I finished a long novel and now I don't know what to read next.
That gap after a good book is a real feeling. What did you like most about the one you finished?
The adventure, and that the main character was a girl who solved problems herself.

Then look for adventure stories with a clever young heroine. Ask your librarian for one, since librarians enjoy this kind of request. You could also try a short book next, as a gentle break before another long one.
My younger sister keeps taking my things without asking.
That's annoying, especially when it's something you care about. What kind of things does she take?
Mostly my pens and my headphones. Sometimes she breaks them.
Breaking them makes it worse. Try talking to her when you're both calm, not right after it happens. Tell her plainly: "Please ask first. When you break my things, it upsets me."
I've tried that. She's eight, she doesn't listen.

At eight, simple rules often work better than talks. You could give her a few old pens of her own, and keep your headphones in a drawer she doesn't open. If it keeps happening, ask your parents to help set a family rule, so you're not the only one enforcing it.
Our new neighbours play loud music late at night, and I have an exam soon.
That's frustrating when you need good sleep before an exam. Has anyone in your family spoken to them yet?
No. My dad says it's awkward to complain.

It doesn't have to sound like a complaint. Someone could knock in the daytime and say, "Welcome to the building. We have exams at home this month. Could you keep the music lower after ten?" Most people respond well to a friendly, specific request.
It's been raining all week and I'm so bored at home.
Long rainy weeks can feel slow. Are you stuck indoors alone, or is someone else at home with you?
My grandfather is here. He mostly reads the newspaper.
Grandparents often have good stories about rainy seasons from long ago. You could ask him what the monsoon was like when he was young, or whether he knows any card games.
He does know a card game! He used to play it with his brothers.
Then ask him to teach you. Learning a game from him is a nice way to spend the afternoon, and he will probably enjoy sharing it. You might hear a few stories about his brothers along the way.
My mom's birthday is next week and I only have a little pocket money.
A gift doesn't need to cost much to mean a lot. What does your mom enjoy?
She likes plants and she likes tea.
Both are good starting points. A small potted plant, like a money plant or a tulsi, costs little and lasts a long time. Or you could make her a card and pair it with her favourite tea.
The plant idea is nice. Should I just give it in the pot from the nursery?
You could paint the pot first. A simple pattern or her name on it makes it personal. Plain clay pots take paint well.
What paint should I use?
The paint you already have for school art will work, like poster colours. Let each coat dry before adding the next. Poster colour can wash off in water, so ask an adult about a clear coat on top.
And what should I write in the card?

Keep it short and from the heart. Mention one thing she does that you're thankful for, like packing your tiffin every morning. For example: "Thank you for all the mornings you get up early for me. Happy birthday, Ma."
I stay up too late every night watching videos on my phone.
A lot of people fall into that habit. Do you want to change it, or is it only bothering you a little?
I want to change it. I'm always tired in the morning.

Then make it easier for yourself. Charge your phone outside your bedroom, or across the room, so it isn't in your hand in bed. Keep a book nearby instead. Pick a fixed time to put the phone away, try it for one week, and see how your mornings feel.
A colleague took credit for my idea in a meeting today.
That's upsetting, especially if you worked hard on it. Did your manager know the idea came from you?
I don't think so. I only told my colleague about it over lunch.
Then it may help to put your ideas in writing next time, like a short email to the team or your manager. That way there is a clear record.
Should I say something to the colleague now?

A calm, private chat is reasonable. You could say, "The idea you shared in the meeting was the one I told you about at lunch. I'd like that to be clear next time." Keep to the facts and avoid blaming words.
And if it happens again?
If it happens again, speak to your manager and show your notes or emails. By then you will have a record, so it isn't just your word against your colleague's.
We're moving to a new city in June and I have to change schools.
That's a big change. Moving can feel exciting and scary at the same time. Which part are you thinking about most?
Making friends. I've been with the same class since I was six.
That makes sense. You've had the same friends for years, so starting over feels strange. The good news is that classes often welcome a new student warmly, especially in the first weeks.
How do I keep my old friends too?

Plan regular calls or messages, maybe once a week, so the friendship doesn't fade. Before you leave, you could pass around a small notebook where each friend writes you a note. And if you visit your old city in the holidays, try to meet them.
I started learning guitar a month ago and my fingertips hurt.
Sore fingertips are normal for beginners. The skin on your fingertips gets tougher with practice, and the soreness usually fades within a few weeks.
Should I practise less then?
Practise in shorter sessions, not less often. Fifteen or twenty minutes a day is better than an hour once a week. Stop when it really hurts, and come back to it the next day.
I want to grow tomatoes on our balcony.
Balcony tomatoes are a nice project. How much sun does your balcony get in a day?
Morning sun only, maybe four hours.
Tomatoes like a lot of sun, usually six hours or more, so four hours may give you a small crop. Cherry tomatoes cope better than big ones. You could also grow mint, which is happy with less sun.
I'll try cherry tomatoes and some mint.
Good mix. Use separate pots, because mint spreads fast and can crowd out other plants. Water when the top of the soil feels dry, and give the tomato plant a stick to lean on as it grows.
I passed my driving test today!
Congratulations! That's a big step. How did the test go?
I was so nervous I stalled the car once, but I still passed.

Stalling once and still passing shows you stayed calm and kept going, and that matters on real roads too. Before any long trips, take a few easy drives with an experienced driver beside you to build confidence.
